questions.title: Valid declarations
questions.question:
Consider the following declarations:

`P: signed short x;`

`Q: unsigned long long int x;`

Which of the given declarations is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution: Both are valid C declarations. `signed short x;` is the same as `short int x;`, and `unsigned long long int x;` is a valid unsigned 64-bit (at least) integer type.

questions.title: 2-byte int overflow
questions.solution: A 2-byte signed `int` holds $-32768$ to $32767$. The value $32769$ does not fit and wraps around: $32769-65536=-32767$.

questions.title: char overflow
questions.solution:
Plain `char` is treated as a signed 8-bit type here (range $-128$ to $127$). $141-256=-115$, so `printf("%d", ch)` prints `-115`.

> Whether plain `char` is signed is implementation-defined; GATE assumes signed.

questions.title: char wrap-around
questions.solution: $-134$ is below $-128$, so it wraps modulo 256: $-134+256=122$. ASCII 122 is `z`.

questions.title: char arithmetic overflow
questions.solution: $125+6=131$ does not fit in a signed `char` (max 127), so it wraps: $131-256=-125$.

questions.title: 2-byte int underflow
questions.solution: $-32769$ is below the 2-byte minimum $-32768$, so it wraps: $-32769+65536=32767$.

questions.title: C standard and sizes
questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:

`P: C standard specifies fixed number of bytes for every data type.`

`Q: The size order for int, short and long data type is short < int < long`

Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution: **P is false:** the standard only gives minimum ranges, so sizes depend on the implementation. **Q is false:** the standard only guarantees `sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long)`; the sizes may be equal, so the strict `<` is not guaranteed.

questions.title: Signed short declarations
questions.question: Which of the following is/are valid declaration of a signed short integer?
questions.solution: All four forms are equivalent. `short`, `short int`, `signed short` and `signed short int` all declare a signed short integer.

questions.title: Mixed int/double expression
questions.solution: `2*6/5` = `12/5` = `2` (integer division). `3.0/2` = `1.5`. So the expression is `2 + 1.5 + 1 = 4.5`. Assigning to an `int` truncates it to `4`, and `%d` prints `4`.

questions.title: % on double
questions.solution: `/`, `*` and `%` have the same precedence and associate left to right: `16.0/4` = `4.0` (double), `4.0*5` = `20.0` (double), then `20.0 % 3` applies `%` to a `double` operand, which is not allowed in C. This is a **compile-time error**.

questions.title: Chained relational operators
Relational vs equality precedence
questions.solution:
Relational operators (`>`, `<`) have higher precedence than equality operators (`!=`). So the expression is `((25>15>0) != (12<45>42)) != 65`.

- `25>15` = `1`, `1>0` = `1`
- `12<45` = `1`, `1>42` = `0`
- `1 != 0` = `1`, then `1 != 65` = `1`

So `a = 1`.

questions.title: Logical AND with assignments
questions.solution: `(a = 5)` is `5` (true), so the right side `(b = 0)` is evaluated: `b` becomes `0` and the value is `0` (false). So `5 && 0` = `0`, which is assigned to `a`. Output: `a = 0`, `b = 0` → `00`.

questions.title: Modulus operator facts
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:

`P: The precedence of the modulus operator is higher than multiplication or division operator.`

`Q: The result of the modulus operator contains the sign of the second operand.`

Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?
questions.solution: **P is incorrect:** `*`, `/` and `%` have the *same* precedence (left to right). **Q is incorrect:** in C99 and later, the result of `%` has the sign of the *first* operand (the dividend), e.g. `-7 % 3 = -1` and `7 % -3 = 1`. So both statements are incorrect.

questions.title: Argument evaluation order
questions.solution:
The order in which function arguments are evaluated is **unspecified** in C. GATE (and common compilers like gcc on x86) evaluate them **right to left**:

1. `a == 2021` → `0` (a is still 2022)
2. `a = 2023` → `2023`
3. `a != 2024` → `1` (a is now 2023)

The values are then printed left to right: `1`, `2023`, `0` → `120230`.

> Strictly, this code is unspecified/undefined behaviour because `a` is read and modified without a sequence point between arguments; the answer assumes right-to-left evaluation.

questions.title: Bitwise NOT
Ternary in if
questions.solution: `i < j` is `2 < 3` = true, so the ternary gives `1`. The `if` condition is true and `GATE` is printed.

questions.title: Assignment in if condition
questions.solution: `a = b - c - d = -1 - 3 + 4 = 0`, so the condition is **false** and the `else` branch runs: `c--` gives `3`, `++a` gives `1`, `++b` gives `0`. Output: `3 1 0`.

questions.title: Nested ternary
questions.solution: `3 > 2` is true, so the value is `(0 ? 0 : 1)` = `1`, giving `a = 1`. `a == a - 1` is `1 == 0` = false, so the `else` branch prints `GATE WALLAH`.

questions.title: printf return value
questions.solution: `printf` returns the number of characters printed. `GATE Wallah 2023` has 16 characters, so `a = 16`. `16 % 4 == 0`, so `a = 21`. `printf("%d", a++)` prints `21` and then `a` becomes `22`.

questions.title: Ternary with post-decrement
Tokenisation a+++--b
Assignment in if
questions.solution: `printf("%d", a)` prints `0`. `a = 2` is an assignment whose value `2` is true, so `Hi` and `2` are printed; the last `printf` prints `2` again. Output: `0Hi22`.

questions.title: Short-circuit OR
questions.solution: `(a = 4)` is true, so `||` **short-circuits** and `(b = 1)` is never evaluated; `b` stays `0`. `a` becomes `1`. `a && b` is `1 && 0` = false, so `PankajSharma` is printed, then `b = 0`. Output: `PankajSharma0`.

questions.title: for with empty body
questions.solution:
Trace of `i` (test `i++ <= 9`, then update `++i`):

| Test sees | `i` after test | After `++i` |
|---|---|---|
| 3 (true) | 4 | 5 |
| 5 (true) | 6 | 7 |
| 7 (true) | 8 | 9 |
| 9 (true) | 10 | 11 |
| 11 (false) | 12 | (loop ends) |

The test increments `i` even when it fails, so `i = 12` is printed.

questions.title: for with break
questions.solution: Value of `i` inside the body in each iteration: 4, 6, 8, 10. `printf` runs in all of them, and the `break` fires at `i = 10` (`10 > 8`). So `printf` executes **4** times.

questions.title: for update printf
questions.solution: The update expression `printf("%d\t", a)` runs *after* each body execution. Body runs: `a` goes 0→1 (b=1), 1→2, 2→3, 3→4 (b=1), 4→5 (`4 <= 3` is false so `b = 0`). The printed values after each body are `1 2 3 4 5`; then the test `b` fails.

questions.title: Loop with i *= 2
questions.solution:
`i` takes the values 2, 4, 8, ..., doubling each time until it exceeds `n`, so the loop runs about $\log_2 n$ times.

> Note: `n` is not declared in the given code. The question is conceptual and assumes an `int n` is available.

questions.title: printf in loop condition
questions.solution: `printf("GATE")` returns `4`, so `i = 4`; `printf("Wallah2023")` always returns `10`. The condition is evaluated each time (printing `Wallah2023` every time), and the values of `i` at the test are: 4 → (even) 3 → (odd) 5 → 7 → 9 → 11. Tests: `4<10`, `3<10`, `5<10`, `7<10`, `9<10`, `11<10`. That is **6** tests, so `Wallah2023` is printed 6 times.

questions.title: Nested loops n^2
questions.solution: Two nested loops each run `n` times, so `printf` executes $n^2 = 32^2 = 1024$ times.

questions.title: Triangular loop count
questions.solution: The inner loop runs `i` times for each `i`, so `count = 1 + 2 + ... + 31 = \dfrac{31 \cdot 32}{2} = 496`.

questions.title: Float to int then %c
questions.solution: `12.5/5 = 2.5`, `31.2/2*5 = 15.6*5 = 78.0`, so the expression is `2.5 + 78 - 5 = 75.5`, stored in an `int` as `a = 75`. The loop prints characters for `i = 75, 78, 81, 84, 87`. Adding 32 gives 107, 110, 113, 116, 119, which are the ASCII characters `k n q t w` (`%c`, not `%d`).

questions.title: while with bitwise AND
questions.solution: `++b` goes 9,10,...; `a--` yields 7,6,...,1,0 (bitwise `&`). Trace: `9&7=1`, `10&6=2`, `11&5=1`, `12&4=4`, `13&3=1`, `14&2=2`, `15&1=1` are all non-zero (7 iterations), then `16&0=0` ends the loop. So `printf` executes **7** times.

questions.title: while with switch
questions.solution:
Trace (`++b` first, then `a--` uses the old value of `a`):

| Test | `++b` | `a--` (old `a`) | `b & a` | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `b = 11` | `5` | `1011 & 0101 = 1` (true) | `switch(11)` → `default`: `b = 8` |
| 2 | `b = 9` | `4` | `1001 & 0100 = 0` (false) | loop ends |

After the loop `a = 3` and `b = 9`. Output: `3 9`.

> **Note:** The source options (3 0, 4 2, 3 2, 4 1) do not contain the correct output `3 9`, so the question is stored as a self-check question. Verified by compiling and running.

questions.title: do-while with inner while
questions.solution:
Start `a = 1`, `b = 2`.

- `while(b++)`: test `2` (true), `b = 3`; body: `b = 3-1 = 2`, `a = 1+2 = 3`.
- `while(b++)`: test `2` (true), `b = 3`; body: `b = 3-3 = 0`, `a = 3+0 = 3`.
- `while(b++)`: test `0` (false), `b = 1`; inner loop ends.
- `while(a++ < 2)`: `3 < 2` is false and `a` becomes `4`.

Output: `a = 4`, `b = 1`.

> **Note:** The source asks for the "number of times printf() executed" but the options are output values, so the question is treated as "The output is".

questions.title: printf return values and switch
questions.solution:
`printf("GATE")` returns 4 and `printf("Wallah")` returns 6 (printed left to right in the expected answer). `4 > 6` is false, so `printf("Hi!!")` runs and returns 4: `a = 4`, `b = 3`.

Loop: `a > b` (`4 > 3`) is true. `switch(3)` goes to `default`: `b = --a`, so `a = 3`, `b = 3`. Now `a > b` is false and the loop ends. Output: `GATEWallahHi!!` followed by `33`.

> The order in which the two `printf` operands of `>` are evaluated is unspecified; the answer assumes left to right.

questions.title: do-while sum
questions.solution: Each pass subtracts 2 and then `i++` (in the test) adds 1, so the printed values are `14, 13, 12, ..., 1, 0`. Sum $= \dfrac{14 \cdot 15}{2} = 105$.

questions.title: Loop count with powers of 2
questions.solution: After $k$ iterations $b = 2^{n+k}$ and $a = 2^{m-k}$. The loop stops when `a == b`, i.e. $n + k = m - k$, so $k = \dfrac{m-n}{2}$. Before that point $b < a$, so the `break` never fires. The loop runs $\dfrac{m-n}{2}$ times.

questions.title: while with printf in if
questions.solution: `printf("GATE")` returns 4, so `4 - 3 = 1` (true) and the `while` loop executes. Inside the body `x` has already been decremented: `x` = 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 are added. `y = 10 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 20`.

questions.title: compound assignment in while
questions.solution: `<` has higher precedence than `-=`, so the loop condition is `x -= (y++ < 10)`. While `y < 10`, `1` is subtracted from `x`: `x` = 4, 3, 2, 1 (non-zero, so the body runs, 4 times). On the 5th test `x` becomes `0`, and the loop stops. So it is printed **4** times.

questions.title: switch fall-through
questions.solution:
`switch(0)` enters `case 0` and falls through (no `break`) into `case 1` and `case 2`: `i = 0+1 = 1`, `i = 1+3 = 4`, `i = 4*2 = 8`, then `break`.

> **Note:** A `printf` was added to the code so the value can be observed; the original program had no output statement.

questions.title: Short-circuit and switch
questions.solution:
`b++ && c--` is `1 && 1` = `1` (then `b = 2`, `c = 0`); because the left side of `||` is true, `d++ && e--` is **not** evaluated, so `d = 2` and `e = -1`. `a = 1`.

`switch(c)` with `c = 0`: `case 0` → `a = 2`, falls into `case 1` → `a = 1`, falls into `default` → `a = -1`.

Sum: `a + b + c + d + e = -1 + 2 + 0 + 2 - 1 = 2`.

> **Note:** A `printf` was added to the code so the sum can be observed.

questions.title: switch default fall-through
questions.solution: `x = -4` matches no case, so `default` runs: `x = -5`, then it falls through to `case 1`: `x = -16`, then `case 2`: `x = 112`, then `break`. ASCII 112 is `p`.

questions.title: switch on expression
questions.solution: `2*3/6 = 1`, `2.0/5 = 0.4`, `0.2*3 = 0.6`, so the sum is `2.0` and `q = 2`. `r = -q--` gives `r = -2` and then `q = 1`. `q - r = 1 - (-2) = 3`, so `case 3` prints `GATE Wallah` and `break` stops.

questions.title: switch with mixed fall-through
questions.solution:
| `j` | case taken | `p` after |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | `default` then `case 3` (−8 −7) | −15 |
| 7 | `default` then `case 3` | −30 |
| 4 | `default` then `case 3` | −45 |
| 1 | `case 1` then `case 2` (+3 +5) | −37 |

Output: `-15 -30 -45 -37`.

questions.title: switch inside for
questions.solution: `x = 0`: falls through all cases: `0+2+5+1+7 = 15`, prints `15`. Then `x++` gives `16` (`default` only): `16+7 = 23`, prints `23`. Then `x++` gives `24`: `24+7 = 31`, prints `31`. Then `x++` gives `32` and the loop ends. Sum: `15 + 23 + 31 = 69`.

questions.title: switch rules
questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:

`P: Case label can be integer or character or floating point numbers.`

`Q: Only one default is allowed in switch-case structure.`

Which of the following statements are INCORRECT?
questions.solution: **P is incorrect:** case labels must be integer constant expressions (integers or characters); floating-point constants are not allowed. **Q is correct:** a `switch` can have at most one `default`. So only P is incorrect.

questions.title: Chained equality
questions.solution:
`==` is left associative: `(x == y) == 5` = `(4 == 5) == 5` = `0 == 5` = `0`, so `x = 0`. `switch(1)` runs `case 1`: `x = 11`. `++x` makes it `12`, which is printed.

> **Note:** The source options (0, 1, 11, Compiler Error) do not contain the correct value 12. The question is therefore stored as a numerical-answer question; verified by compiling and running.

questions.title: Nested function calls
questions.solution: `f2(5) = 5*5 = 25` and `f1(5) = 5*f2(5) = 125`. Each iteration does `b -= 125 - 25 = 100`: first `b = 4 - 100 = -96`, then `b = -196`. The sum of printed values is `-96 + (-196) = -292`.

questions.title: Function declarations and loop
options: "GATE Wallah" will be printed infinite number of times.
questions.solution: The repeated block-scope declarations `void print();` are legal (they declare the function with unspecified parameters). In `print(-9)`: `n++` (init) gives `-8`. Test `n++`: values -8, -6, -4, -2 are non-zero and each pass prints; the test `n++` that sees `0` ends the loop. So it is printed **4** times.

questions.title: Shift vs plus precedence
questions.solution: `+` has higher precedence than `<<`, so `n << 1 + n` = `n << (1 + n)` = `1 << 2` = `4`. `case 4` prints `Parakram`, falls through to `case 3` and prints `2024`, then `break`.

questions.title: Nested ternary with printf
questions.solution: `10 < 5` is false, so the second operand is skipped. The third operand is `printf("") ? printf("2024") : printf("%d", printf("Wallah Parakram"))`. `printf("")` returns `0` (false), so the last part runs: the inner `printf` prints `Wallah Parakram` (15 chars) and returns `15`, then the outer prints `15`.

questions.title: Shift and post-decrement
Side effects in for header
questions.solution: `r(x)` only returns `x - 1` and does not change the caller's variable, so the side effects come from `n++` and `--n`. Trace: test `r(n++)` (n=4→5, returns 3, true) → body `r(--n)` (n=4, prints `3`) → update `--n` (n=3) → test (passes 3, n=4, returns 2) → body (n=3, prints `2`) → update (n=2) → test (passes 2, n=3, returns 1) → body (n=2, prints `1`) → update (n=1) → test (passes 1, returns 0) stops. Output: `3 2 1`.

questions.title: static initialiser must be constant
questions.solution: A `static` variable must be initialised with a **constant expression**. `a++` is not a constant, so this is a compile-time error.

questions.title: Multiple extern declarations
questions.solution: Repeating an `extern` declaration is legal. All three refer to the global `a` defined below with the value `15`.

questions.title: Static variables across calls
Static local variable
questions.solution: In `f`, `a` is static (keeps its value) and `b` is re-created as `5` on each call. Call 1: `a = 3 - 5 = -2`, `b = 6` → `-2 6`. Call 2: `a = -2 - 5 = -7`, `b = 6` → `-7 6`. In `main`, `a = 2 + 3 = 5`, `b = 1` → `5 1`.

questions.title: extern and static i
questions.solution: `'B' = 66`. The two calls return `2` and `3` (the static `i` inside `f`). In `main`, `extern int i` refers to the global `i = 1`. Sum `66 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 72` (order of evaluation does not matter here).

questions.title: static global j
questions.solution: `static int j;` followed by `static int j = 3;` is a legal tentative definition. First call: `i++ + --j` = `2 + 2` = `4` (`j = 2`). Second call: `2 + 1` = `3` (`j = 1`). Total: `66 + 4 + 3 = 73`.

questions.title: Counting printf calls
questions.solution: `f()` returns 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, ... The initialisation call consumes `5`. The test calls return `4, 3, 2, 1` (true, 4 iterations) and then `0` (false). In each of the 4 iterations the body `printf` and the update `printf` both execute: `4 + 4 = 8` calls.

questions.title: Storage class facts
questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
options: A static variable has internal linkage.
Static variables are stored in the data segment.
Auto variables are stored in the heap segment.
Register variables behave as auto variables by default.
questions.solution: (a) is not true in general: only a *file-scope* `static` variable has internal linkage; a `static` local variable has no linkage. (b) is correct: static (and global) variables live in the data/BSS segment. (c) is false: auto variables live on the **stack**, not the heap. (d) is correct: `register` is only a hint, and when no register is available the variable behaves like an auto variable.

questions.title: Recursive division
static then extern
questions.solution: `static int i;` followed by `extern int i = 3;` refers to the same variable (the `extern` keeps the earlier internal linkage) and initialises it to `3`. `f(4)` prints the current `i` and increments it 4 times: `3 4 5 6`.

questions.title: Recursion with static
Two-argument recursion
Recursion tree output
questions.solution:
Expanding the recursion for `arc(7)`:

- `arc(5)` prints: `arc(3)` → (`arc(1)` nothing) `2`, (`arc(0)` nothing) `1`; then `4`; `arc(2)` nothing; then `3`.
- Back in `arc(7)`: prints `6`.
- `arc(4)` prints: `arc(2)` nothing; `3`; `arc(1)` nothing; `2`.
- Back in `arc(7)`: prints `5`.

Output: `2 1 4 3 6 3 2 5` → `21436325`.

questions.title: Recursion count
options: "GATE Wallah" will be printed infinite number of times.
questions.solution: Each call prints once. The values received are `-4, -3, -2, -1, 0`: in every call `n++` moves `n` by one and the recursive call receives `n` (the second `n++` only affects the local copy), so each level passes `n + 1`. The call with `n = 0` returns after printing. That is **5** prints.

questions.title: static b in recursion
questions.solution: `b` is static and keeps increasing; `a` is a fresh copy of `b` in each call. Each call prints `a` and `b` (both equal), then `a = b + 1`. The recursion continues while `a <= 3`: output `0 0 1 1 2 2 3 3`.

questions.title: Nested recursion
Static b recursion
Recursion with printf
questions.solution:
`func(0)` prints `-1`. `func(1)` then prints `1` and `0`. `func(2)` then prints `2` and `1`. Output: `-1 1 0 2 1` → `-11021`.

> **Source note:** the code in your source had both `printf` calls inside the `if` block, which would print `1 0 2 1`, but none of the options match that. The code above (second `printf` after the `if`, as in your practice question `rc-10`) matches the options. Options (a) and (d) are identical in the source; (a) is marked.

questions.title: Two recursive calls
Recursion with n/4
Static k in recursion
questions.solution:
Calls go `func(8) → func(4) → func(2) → func(1) → func(0)`; `k` becomes `1, 2, 3, 4` on the way down. `func(0)` returns `0 + k--` = `4` and sets `k = 3`. Unwinding (`k` read *after* the recursive call, as gcc evaluates it): `func(1) = 2*4 + 3 = 11`, `func(2) = 2*11 + 3 = 25`, `func(4) = 2*25 + 3 = 53`, `func(8) = 2*53 + 3 = 109`.

> The order of evaluating `func(n/2)` and `k` in `2 * func(n/2) + k` is unspecified in C; the answer follows gcc.

questions.title: Binary recursion
Static i in recursion
questions.solution:
`i` is static. `func(7)`: `7/2 = 3` is non-zero, `i = -1`, calls `func(3)`. `func(3)`: `3/2 = 1`, `i = -2`, calls `func(1)`. `func(1)`: `1/2 = 0`, so it returns `i = -2`. Unwinding: `func(3) = -2 + i = -2 + (-2) = -4` and `func(7) = -4 + i = -4 + (-2) = -6`, where `i` is read after the recursive call (the order is unspecified; gcc reads it after).

Result: `-6`.

questions.title: Static counter and printf
questions.solution: `printf("GATE24")` always returns `6`. The first call of `display()` prints (static `i = 0`), then sets `i = 2`, 4, 6, 8: it prints at `i = 0, 2, 4, 6` (all `<= 6`) and once more at `i = 8` (not `<= 6`, so it stops): 5 prints. The 2nd and 3rd calls from `main` each print once (static `i` is already 8). Total: `5 + 1 + 1 = 7`.

questions.title: Invalid array declarations
questions.question: Which of the following declarations are INVALID?
questions.solution: Only the **first** dimension may be omitted, and only when an initialiser is given (the compiler counts the elements). (a) and (b) have no initialiser, so the size is unknown, and (c) omits a middle dimension; these are invalid. (d) is valid: it becomes `b[1][2][2]`.

questions.title: Array name vs pointer
questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:

`P: int a[3]={1,2,3}; printf("%d", *a++);`

`Q: int a[3]={1,2,3}; int *p=a; printf("%d", *p++);`

Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
The array name `a` is not a modifiable lvalue, so `a++` in P is a compile-time error. In Q, `p` is a pointer variable, so `*p++` is valid and prints `1`. Only Q is correct.

> **Note:** The source gave no options; the standard four options were added.

questions.title: Index swap a[1] == 1[a]
Index swap (repeat)
questions.solution:
`1[a]` = `*(1 + a)` = `a[1]` = `10`.

> **Note:** This question is identical to the previous one in the source (the source declaration had a typo `int 5[a]`). Kept as given.

questions.title: Pointer arithmetic with base address
&a + 1
Array of pointers
Array of pointers dereference
questions.solution:
`arr` is an array of `int*`. Line 1: `*(arr+1)` is `b`, so `*(b+2) = b[2] = 5` (valid). Line 2: `**arr` is `a[0] = 2`, so `**arr + 3 = 5` (valid). Line 3: `***arr` dereferences an `int`, which is an error.

> **Note:** The source gave no options; one option per line was added.

questions.title: Recursive array pointer function
questions.solution: For each call `i = n-1`, so it prints `p[n-1] + p[0]`: `5+1 = 6`, `4+1 = 5`, `3+1 = 4`, `2+1 = 3`, `1+1 = 2`; then `n = 0` gives `i = -1` and it returns. Output: `6 5 4 3 2`.

questions.title: Pointer to pointer
Pointer to array row
questions.solution: `ptr` points to row 0. `**ptr += 1` increments `arr[0][0]` from `0` to `1`. `ptr++` moves to row 1. `**ptr *= 3` makes `arr[1][0] = 2 * 3 = 6`. Final array: `{{1,1},{6,3}}`.

questions.title: 3-D array pointer arithmetic
questions.solution: `a` is `int[2][3][2]`. `a+1` skips one `int[3][2]` (12 bytes): `112`. `*a+1` skips one `int[2]` (4 bytes): `104`. `**a+1` skips one `int` (2 bytes): `102`. `***a+1` is `a[0][0][0] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2`. `&a+1` skips the whole array (24 bytes): `124`.

questions.title: ptr += sizeof(int)
questions.solution: `sizeof(int) = 2`, so `ptr += 2` moves two `int`s forward from `a[0][0]`, reaching `a[1][0] = 5`.

questions.title: ++*ptr++
questions.solution: `a[1]` is `{5, 7}`, so `ptr` points to `5`. In `++*ptr++`, the postfix `ptr++` binds first (the pointer moves to `7` after the expression), then `*` accesses `5` and the prefix `++` increments that value to `6`. Finally `*ptr` is `7`.

questions.title: Invalid double dereference
questions.solution: `q` is an `int*`, so `*q` is an `int` and `**q` dereferences an integer, which is an invalid operand. This is a **compile-time error** (`invalid type argument of unary '*'`).

questions.title: Returning pointer to static array
questions.solution: `a` is static, so it still exists after `f` returns. The loop prints `1+2 = 3`, `2+3 = 5`, `3+4 = 7`.

questions.title: Pointer to pointer arithmetic
questions.solution:
`*q = p++ + *q` modifies `p` and also reads `*q` (which is `p`) without a sequence point, so this is unspecified/undefined behaviour in C. With gcc, `p++` makes `p = 11` and `*q` is then read as `11`, so `p = 10 + 11 = 21`.

Then `q = &s`, `r = &q`. `**r = -*q***r` is `(-*q) * (**r)` = `-20 * 20 = -400`, so `s = -400`.

`p + s = 21 + (-400) = -379`.

> **Note:** Unspecified order of evaluation in `p++ + *q`; the answer follows gcc.

questions.title: Returning pointer to local array
questions.solution: `a` is a local array; it is destroyed when `f` returns, so `p` is a **dangling pointer**. Reading through it is undefined behaviour and prints garbage (or crashes). The compiler normally warns `function returns address of local variable`.

questions.title: Complex declarations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:

`P: int * p(int *)` - p is a function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer pointer.

`Q: int (*p(int *))[]` - p is a function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns a pointer to an array of integers.

Which of the following is INCORRECT?
questions.solution:
Both descriptions are correct. In P, `p` is a function `(int*) -> int*`. In Q, `p(int *)` is a function, `*p(int *)` is its (pointer) return value, and `(...)[]` makes it a pointer to an array of `int`. So *neither* statement is incorrect.

> **Note:** The source gave no options; the standard four options were added.

questions.title: Pointer to array of 2 ints
questions.solution: `q` points to row 0 `{2,4}`, so `(*q)[1] = 4`. `q += 2` moves two rows to `{10,12}`, so `(*q)[1] = 12`.

questions.title: &a + 1 as int pointer
questions.solution: `*(a+1) = a[1] = 1`. `&a+1` points one whole array past `a`, so `p` points just after `a[2]`, and `*(p-1) = a[2] = 2`. Output: `1 2`.

questions.title: Function pointer with loop
questions.solution: `n = 6`. Init: `n--` gives `5`. Test `--n` = `4` (true) → print. Update `--n` = `3`. Test `--n` = `2` (true) → print. Update `--n` = `1`. Test `--n` = `0` (false) → stop. So `GATE WALLAH` is printed twice.

questions.title: void pointer dereference
questions.question:
Consider the following codes:

`P: void *p; p = malloc(1); *p = 65; printf("%c",*(char*)p);`

`Q: void *p; char a='A'; p = malloc(1); p = &a; printf("%c",*(char*)p);`

Which of the following is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
In P, `*p = 65` dereferences a `void *`, which is an error (it must be cast first). Q compiles and prints `A` (the `malloc`ed memory is leaked, but that is not an error). Only Q is correct.

> **Note:** The source gave no options; the standard four options were added.

questions.title: Heap vs local address
questions.solution:
Line 1 returns a heap address from `malloc`, which stays valid. Line 2 returns the address of the parameter `a`, a local variable that is destroyed when `g` returns, so the pointer is **dangling** (incorrect).

> **Note:** The source gave no options; one option per line was added.

questions.title: Reading int via char pointer
questions.solution: `324 = 0x144`. The first (lowest-address) byte on a little-endian machine is `0x44 = 68`. Casting the pointer to `char*` reads that single byte, so `68` is printed.

questions.title: malloc loop
realloc and uninitialised bytes
questions.answer: A followed by an unpredictable (garbage) integer
questions.solution: `*p = 65` prints `A`. After `realloc` to 4 bytes the first byte is assigned `256`, which does not fit in a `char` and becomes `0`. Reading the 4 bytes as an `int` also reads 3 **uninitialised** bytes, so the integer is not guaranteed (it is `0` only if that memory happens to be zero). The output is `A` followed by an unpredictable number.

questions.title: static and malloc pointers
questions.solution: `g` returns the address of a `static` variable (still valid) → `10`. `f` returns a pointer to `malloc`ed memory → `20`. Output: `10 20`.

questions.title: malloc failure
questions.question: When the memory is full, `malloc` returns:
questions.solution: `malloc` returns `NULL` when it cannot allocate the requested memory. (On success it returns a `void *`, but on failure the returned value is the null pointer.)

questions.title: calloc zero initialisation
questions.solution: `calloc` zero-initialises the memory, so the first two prints show `0 0`. After the assignments the values are `10 15`. Output: `0 0 10 15`.

questions.title: Modifying string literals
questions.solution: A string literal lives in read-only memory, and modifying it is undefined behaviour (usually a segmentation fault). P modifies it through `p`, and Q modifies the same literal through `q`. Both are incorrect: **2**.

questions.title: Array comparison
questions.solution: P compares the **addresses** of two different arrays, which are never equal, so it prints `NO`. Q compares the first characters `'G'` and `'G'`, which are equal, so it prints `YES`.

questions.title: scanf %s vs gets
questions.solution:
`scanf("%s")` stops at the first whitespace, so P reads only `CS`. `gets` reads the whole line, so Q prints `CS 2023`.

> `gets` was removed in C11 and is unsafe; this question is based on the older standard.

questions.title: Pointer offset and null terminator
questions.solution: `s + 4` points to `Wallah`, so that is printed first. Then `s[4] = 0` terminates the string after `GATE`, and the second `printf` prints `GATE`. Output: `WallahGATE`.

questions.title: Pointer + char arithmetic
questions.solution: `s[3] = 'E' = 69` and `s[1] = 'A' = 65`, so the offset is `4` and the string starts at `Wallah...`. `s[10] = '0'` replaces the `'2'` at index 10 (`GATEWallah` has 10 characters, so index 10 is the first digit). The tail becomes `Wallah0023`.

questions.title: Static index string update
questions.solution:
`q` is static: calls modify indices 5, 8 and 11. `p[5] = 'a'+2 = 'c'`, `p[8] = 'a'+2 = 'c'`, `p[11] = 'e'+2 = 'g'`. Result: `GATEWcllchbgsthai`.

> Options (c) and (d) are identical in the source.

questions.title: Recursive string printing
questions.solution: The first `printf` runs before the recursive call (forward order `GATE`); the second runs after it (reverse order `ETAG`). Output: `GATEETAG`.

questions.title: strcmp and printf return
questions.solution: The two strings are equal, so `strcmp` returns `0` and the `if` runs. `printf("GATEWallah")` returns the number of characters printed, `10`, so `a = 10`.

questions.title: &5[a]
questions.solution: `5[a]` is `a[5]`, so `&5[a]` is `a + 5`, which points to `Wallah`. Both `printf`s print `Wallah`, separated by a tab.

questions.title: Array assignment
questions.solution: An array name is not a modifiable lvalue, so an array cannot be assigned with `=`. This is a **compile-time error** (use `strcpy` instead).

questions.title: strcmp ternary
questions.solution: `strcmp("abcd", "acd")` is non-zero (`b` vs `c`), so the ternary picks `strlen(p) = 4`.

questions.title: Pointer to pointer to string
questions.solution: `q = p + 3`. `q[-2]` is `p[1] = s+4`, and `q[-2][-1]` is `s[3] = "ELECTRICAL"`, which is printed. Then `q = q - 2` = `p+1`. `***q` is `*(*(*q))`: `*q = s+4`, `**q = s[4] = "CIVIL"`, `***q = 'C'`, so `'C' + 1 = 'D'`. Output: `ELECTRICALD`.

questions.title: strlen vs sizeof
questions.solution: `strcpy` copies the 8 characters plus the null terminator (9 bytes) into `b[9]`. `strlen(b) = 8`, and `sizeof(b) = 9` (the array size). Output: `GATE2024` + `8` + `9`.

questions.title: Skip-one recursion
questions.solution: The function prints every second character: indices 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → `G`, `T`, `W`, `l`, `a`. The next pointer (index 10) is the null terminator. Output: `GTWla`.

questions.title: Terminating a string through a pointer
questions.solution: `p` points to index 4. Writing `'\0'` there makes `p` point at a null terminator, so `printf("%s", p)` prints an empty string: no output.

questions.title: Pointer chain with ++/--
questions.solution: `++c` makes `c = b+1`, so `*++c = b[1]`. `--*++c` decrements `b[1]` from `a+3` to `a+2`; `*` of that is `a[2] = "Wallah"`, and `+ 3` gives `"lah"`, printed first. Then `++c` makes `c = b+2`, `*c = b[2] = a+1`, `**c = a[1] = "Parakram"`. Output: `lahParakram`, of length `3 + 8 = 11`.

questions.title: Union size
questions.solution: A union takes the size of its largest member: `double d[2]` = `2 × 4 = 8` bytes.

questions.title: Struct containing a union
questions.solution:
`long a[3]` takes `3 × 8 = 24` bytes. The union takes the larger of `int` (2) and `float` (4) = `4` bytes. Total: `24 + 4 = 28` bytes.

> This ignores alignment padding (the expected GATE answer). On a real machine with 8-byte alignment the struct would be padded to 32 bytes.

questions.title: Struct passed by pointer
questions.solution: `f` receives a **pointer**, so the original struct is modified: `a = 'A'+2 = 'C'` and `b = 'C'-1 = 'B'`. Output: `C` then `B`.

questions.title: Struct passed by value
questions.solution: The struct is passed **by value**, so `f` changes only its own copy. `main`'s `s1` stays `A` and `C`.

questions.title: Static counter updating struct
questions.solution:
`f(s1)` works on a copy, so `s1` stays `A`, `C`. `g` updates `s2` through a pointer; `count` is static (starts at 2):

- Call 1: `a += 2` (count becomes 3) → `'B'+2 = 'D'`; `b += ++count` (count = 4) → `'D'+4 = 'H'`.
- Call 2: `a += 4` (count becomes 5) → `'D'+4 = 'H'`; `b += ++count` (count = 6) → `'H'+6 = 'N'`.

Output: `A C H N` → `ACHN`.

questions.title: Pointer and struct operator precedence
questions.solution: `p = s+3` (Wednesday). `*p++->q`: `p++->q` uses the old `p` and then moves `p` to Thursday; `*` gives the first character `W`. Next, `*++p->q` is `*(++(p->q))`: it increments Thursday's string pointer to `"hursday"` and prints `h`. Then `p = p - 2` points to Tuesday, so `%s` prints `Tuesday`. Output: `WhTuesday`.

questions.title: Structure rules
questions.question: Which of the following statements are INCORRECT?
options: Functions cannot be defined inside the structure.
Structure variable of the same structure type can be defined inside a structure.
A function may not contain a structure defined in it.
Existing structure cannot be contained in another structure.
questions.solution: (a) is a **correct** statement (C structs cannot contain function definitions, only function pointers). (b) is incorrect: a struct cannot contain a member of its own type (it would be infinitely large), only a pointer to it. (c) is incorrect: a struct can be defined inside a function. (d) is incorrect: structures can be nested. So (b), (c) and (d) are the incorrect statements.

questions.title: Array member assignment
questions.solution: Only line b is an error: an array member cannot be assigned with `=` (use `strcpy`). Line a (`strcpy`) is fine. Lines c and d compile fine (d prints an uninitialised string, which is a runtime issue, not a compile error). So **1** line has an error.

questions.title: Static vs dynamic scoping
questions.solution:
**Static scoping:** `g` looks up `i` where `g` is *defined*, i.e. the global `i = 10`, so `x = 10`. **Dynamic scoping:** `g` looks up `i` along the *call chain* (`main → f → g`); the nearest `i` is `f`'s local `i = 20`, so `y = 20`.

> The source did not state what to compute from `x` and `y`; for example `x + y = 30` and `y - x = 10`.
